title: Dust: Pretraining Transformers Without Backpropagation
author: Samip Dahal, Bishwas Mandal, Serdar Gülbahar, Akshay Vegesna (Q Labs)
takeaway: A research post with code: Dust adds independent noise to each layer's activations at every token, credits each token's noise with that token's own loss change, and forms the weight update as backprop does (estimated error times input); on a 37.7M-parameter GPT trained with constant-rate SGD (three seeds per cell), 16,384 draws per update end slightly below backprop at 100k and 1M tokens (6 and 61 updates) and 0.06 and 0.17 above it at 10M and 20M, at about 5,000 times backprop's compute per update by our count, while the authors' weight-space ES baseline would need an extrapolated 3,000 to 23,000 times the population to match Dust's smallest setting.
verdict: Believe the mechanism and its large lead over weight-space ES. Read "competitive with backprop" narrowly: the measured wins are at 6 and 61 updates against constant-rate SGD, the gap widens as training lengthens, the sub-backprop figure at 20M tokens is a fitted extrapolation, the lab's own benchmark puts Dust 0.40 behind once both use Adam, and an update costs thousands of backprop updates.

headline.k: what the authors' weight-space ES baseline (EGGROLL-Transformer) would need to match Dust at 64 draws, extrapolated from runs at 64 to 16k; the post rounds it to 10^3 to 10^4
headline.at: Weight-space ES is far less efficient.

code.n: Created 2 October, last commit 6 October 2026 (b20f7c0): dust.py (the estimator with its tuned per-population allocations and the training loop), model.py, a backprop SGD baseline, data preparation and the BPE-4096 tokenizer. A minimal version that "omits execution optimizations used in the full experiments", for the 1M and 10M budgets at 256 to 16,384 draws on one to eight GPUs. No logs, checkpoints or result files, and no code for EGGROLL, Adam, the model-size study or the cosine measurements. Two open issues on 27 November, neither answered.

more_note: Sections 2 (Method) and 3.2 (Main Results) carry the argument; the appendix (about 11 minutes) holds Table 1 with every loss, the extrapolation behind the 10^3 to 10^4 claim, the draw allocation and the tuning protocol.

discussion.t: Hacker News: Dust: Pretraining Transformers Without Backpropagation

responses.t: Hacker News: the gradient tells you where to go
responses.n: The top comment bets no derivative-free optimiser will matter for neural networks: their objectives are smooth, and the gradient's edge over random directions grows with the parameter count. A reply notes the gradient-free complexity gap it cites is textbook, not new. Neither engages with per-token credit.

responses.t: Hacker News: is this a bitter-lesson method at all?
responses.n: Argues that zeroth-order estimates smooth the loss without addressing non-convexity, that the post never discusses convexity, and that better first-order methods will keep the lead wherever gradients exist.

responses.t: Hacker News: parallel along depth, and less memory
responses.by: SerdarGl (co-author Serdar Gülbahar) and nbutton762, Hacker News
responses.n: The co-author's one reply: at massive scale zeroth-order methods "will parallelize better than backprop especially along depth" (pipelines without bubbles). Another commenter adds that Dust stores only each layer's inputs. Neither is measured in the post.

responses.t: How to read the claim that Dust trained without backpropagation
responses.n: The one careful outside reading: it counts the updates (about 6, 61, 610, 1,221), tabulates Dust minus backprop (-0.046, -0.043, +0.060, +0.169), notes every measured Adam point sits above backprop (best 5.368 against 5.361), and finds no compute or wall-clock figures.

responses.t: The backprop breakthrough with a massive catch
responses.n: The catch is compute: token-level parallelism reallocates GPU-hours rather than saving them. Every number is the post's own; its body ("surpassed tuned backpropagation") is stronger than its own FAQ ("in some short training runs").

responses.t: Noise: a speedrun for pretraining without backpropagation
responses.n: A week later the authors benchmarked the 10M-token setting with both optimisers (validation loss, one run each, 8xH100): Dust with SGD 5.058 in 1 h 19 min against backprop's 5.007; with Adam 4.167 against 3.769. Their summary: Dust "rivals backprop under SGD" but "still trails backprop under Adam".

since.n: In ten days outside entrants took the validation-loss track from 4.167 (Dust with Adam) to 3.676, past backprop with Adam (3.769), and the speedrun to loss 4.2 from 1 h 46 min to 1.6 s. The fast entries replace Dust's random draws with structured probes (a Hadamard cycle measuring every neuron's credit at every token; credit handed down from the top of the network), allowed because a measured error may take one step through a nonlinearity: Dust's successors, not Dust.

From 22 October the benchmark trains on 30M tokens. Dust with Adam at 24k draws scores 3.767 in 5 h 17 min against backprop with Adam's 3.419; the best forward-only entry, 3.300, is below that, though backprop with a stronger optimiser (ANVIL II) scores 3.340. One run each, scored by the repository's own script.

since.t: Q Labs Dust and Noise: is the 4,000x claim verified?
since.n: Checks the viral "4,000x faster" figure: the arithmetic holds (1.76 h to 1.6 s), but it is a community speedrun to a loose target (4.2, where backprop with Adam reaches 3.769), and "the fast entries are not Dust as published".

resources.n: The weight-space baseline: low-rank weight perturbations that make large populations cheap on GPUs. The post re-implements it on its own transformer (EGGROLL-Transformer) rather than running the paper's code.

resources.t: Learning curves for stochastic gradient descent in linear feedforward networks
resources.n: Node perturbation against weight perturbation and backprop on linear networks: the journal version (Neural Computation, 2005) states that node perturbation learns slower than gradient descent by a factor of the number of output units, and weight perturbation slower again by the number of input units; the toy on this page lands on both factors.

resources.t: Evolution strategies as a scalable alternative to reinforcement learning
resources.by: Salimans, Ho, Chen, Sidor and Sutskever, arXiv 1703.03864
resources.n: The modern weight-space ES recipe (antithetic Gaussian perturbations, fitness shaping, a shared seed so workers exchange only scalars) that EGGROLL scales up.

resources.t: Fine-tuning language models with just forward passes (MeZO)
resources.n: The best-known zeroth-order result for language models: fine-tuning, not pretraining, with one random weight direction per step and memory close to inference.

resources.t: Scaling forward gradient with local losses
resources.by: Ren, Kornblith, Liao and Hinton, ICLR 2023
resources.n: Activation perturbation with forward-mode derivatives and local losses to cut the estimator's variance; the closest earlier attempt to make perturbation scale with width.

kb.n: Owns the outer product Dust reuses (a weight gradient is the arriving error times the stored input), forward against reverse mode, and why a backward pass costs about two forwards.
Owns SGD with momentum, Adam and the evidence that a challenger's gain shrinks against a tuned baseline: the lens for Dust's SGD-only headline.
Owns the score-function estimator: reward times noise over sigma is REINFORCE for a Gaussian policy, with a baseline to cut variance.
Where real pretraining budgets sit: Dust's largest run, 20M tokens, is about one ten-thousandth of a small modern pretraining run.

kb.n: An article on looped transformers, the kind of model the post names as a future use: recurrence that backpropagation through time struggles to train.
